articles.title: How researchers debunked ‘race science’: ‘a triumph of scientific self-correction’
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03507-zAn account of how nineteenth-century studies aiming to find a biological basis for human races were dismantled by good scientific practices — although their effects are still felt today.
articles.content:
Civil-rights activist W. E. B. Du Bois.Credit: Bettmann/Getty

The Ends of Race: The Rise and Fall of a Scientific Myth Geoffrey Galt Harpham Princeton University Press (2026)

Two stories about the history of science around race emerge from the nineteenth century. Each tugs at our attention in a different way. Humanities scholar Geoffrey Galt Harpham chronicles them in a book with enthralling detail.

The Ends of Race tracks the decades spent by scientists and scholars intending to prove that human races were distinct, using methods such as measuring skulls and facial forms to set them in biologically fixed categories and develop taxonomies to rank humanity.

Why Africans should be telling the story of human origins

The first set of protagonists, including US anthropologist Josiah Nott and French anthropologist Julien-Joseph Virey, likened Black people’s skulls to ape skulls with evidence as threadbare as a spiderweb, intentionally pushing Black people down the ladder of desirable cultures. It was a myth born to provide cover for racism, Harpham writes.

The second story starts in 1900, during a tide-turning moment for science. Scholars began publishing studies countering the oppressive theories of race scientists. Ultimately, the discrediting of the concept of biological race emerged as a triumph of scientific self-correction.

These stories serve as a potent reminder of not just how science can get it so wrong, but how flawed research can eventually be quashed by sensible approaches. In the case of race, inaccuracies were sustained solely by political and social ends.

As with any good story, the author confidently guides us through a heady mix of characters. And Harpham even contends that this tragic era in science offers a happy ending. Once natural science had dismissed race as a biological reality, authors such as W. E. B. Du Bois took the opportunity to reframe race as a social and cultural identity, to invite solidarity among Black people.

Misplaced taxonomy

The scientific muddling of race and species, and its lasting effect on perpetuating division, has its roots with Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus. His 1735 book Systema Naturae categorized every kind of organism, a magnificent feat at the time. But this process encouraged questions about divisions among humans, similar to what Linnaeus saw in other species.

This area of research excited the scientific community. Early race theorists, such as Nott, clamoured for the “magnificent opportunity to establish the ability of empirical research and scientific method to engage with issues whose interest and importance could be immediately grasped by the public and even valued by the state”, Harpham writes.

Physician Petrus Camper proposed that the angle between the jaw and forehead could differentiate species, a theory used in scientific racism. Credit: Antiqua Print Gallery/Alamy

Nott took Linneaus’s categorization a step further, arguing that human races were not just environmental varieties of a single family, but separate, fixed species created independently by God. He thought that interbreeding between “remote” races led to weak, disease-prone and infertile offspring, and applied mortality data to his claim that Black people in the United States enjoyed joyous lives under Southern chattel slavery but perished in freedom in cold Northern cities.

You can imagine Harpham’s eyes rolling when he shares Nott’s racist views, but he recognizes that these ideas weren’t just the provenance of one man. US physician Samuel George Morton published work in the 1830s in which he expanded on his theory that skull size and shape reflected brain size and intellectual capacity. He ranked racial cultures on their mean cranial size: Caucasians at the number-one position, followed by Mongolians, Malays, Native Americans and Ethiopians (a catch-all term for Black people) at the bottom.

How ‘organized looting and plunder’ drove Britain’s second scientific revolution

The context of slavery is necessary to fully understand some of these outlandish studies, Harpham stresses. Both Nott and Morton argued that since the time of ancient Egypt, enslaver–enslaved relationships and the physical racial features of each of these groups had remained unchanged, pointing to racial hierarchies laid out as permanent laws of nature rather than temporary social conceptions. At the time, there was little pushback. After all, enslavers benefited from these notions.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the significant scientific and social progress made in debunking the false biological basis of race, which historically justified racism and oppression. It emphasizes the triumph of scientific self-correction and the reframing of race as a social and cultural identity, promoting solidarity and human rights. This represents a meaningful, broad impact on society by challenging and correcting harmful myths that have influenced social policies and attitudes.
articles.personality_title: How science corrected false ideas about race from the 19th century
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In the 1800s, scientists tried to prove that human races were biologically different by measuring skulls and physical features. These ideas were used to support racism and slavery.

**What happened** – A new book by Geoffrey Galt Harpham explains how these early studies were flawed and how later scientists showed that race is not a biological fact. Instead, race is a social and cultural idea. This change happened around 1900 when researchers used better methods to challenge old racist theories.

**Impact** – This story shows how science can fix its mistakes over time. It also helped stop false ideas that justified unfair treatment of people based on race. After science rejected biological race, thinkers like W. E. B. Du Bois helped people understand race as part of culture and identity, encouraging unity instead of division.

**What's next step** – Understanding this history can help society continue to reject racism based on false science. It also reminds us to be careful with research and to question ideas that may be influenced by politics or prejudice.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists corrected harmful 19th-century myths about race, proving it is a social idea, not a biological fact.
articles.personality_title_fr: Comment la science a corrigé les fausses idées sur la race au XIXe siècle
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Au 19e siècle, des scientifiques ont tenté de prouver que les races humaines étaient différentes biologiquement en mesurant des crânes et des traits physiques. Ces idées servaient à justifier le racisme et l'esclavage.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Un nouveau livre de Geoffrey Galt Harpham explique comment ces études anciennes étaient erronées et comment des scientifiques plus tardifs ont montré que la race n'est pas un fait biologique, mais une idée sociale et culturelle. Ce changement s'est produit vers 1900, lorsque des chercheurs ont utilisé de meilleures méthodes pour contester les anciennes théories racistes.

**Impact** – Cette histoire montre comment la science peut corriger ses erreurs avec le temps. Elle a aussi aidé à arrêter les fausses idées qui justifiaient un traitement injuste des personnes selon leur race. Après que la science a rejeté la race biologique, des penseurs comme W. E. B. Du Bois ont aidé à comprendre la race comme une partie de la culture et de l'identité, encourageant l'unité plutôt que la division.

**Prochaine étape** – Comprendre cette histoire peut aider la société à continuer de rejeter le racisme basé sur de fausses sciences. Cela rappelle aussi de rester vigilant face à la recherche influencée par la politique ou les préjugés.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les scientifiques ont corrigé les mythes nocifs du XIXe siècle sur la race, prouvant qu’il s’agit d’une idée sociale, non d’un fait biologique.
articles.personality_title_es: Cómo la ciencia corrigió falsas ideas sobre la raza en el siglo XIX
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En el siglo XIX, científicos intentaron demostrar que las razas humanas eran diferentes biológicamente midiendo cráneos y rasgos físicos. Estas ideas se usaron para justificar el racismo y la esclavitud.

**Qué pasó** – Un nuevo libro de Geoffrey Galt Harpham explica cómo esos estudios antiguos estaban equivocados y cómo científicos posteriores mostraron que la raza no es un hecho biológico, sino una idea social y cultural. Este cambio ocurrió alrededor de 1900, cuando investigadores usaron mejores métodos para desafiar las viejas teorías racistas.

**Impacto** – Esta historia muestra cómo la ciencia puede corregir sus errores con el tiempo. También ayudó a detener ideas falsas que justificaban el trato injusto hacia las personas según su raza. Después de que la ciencia rechazó la raza biológica, pensadores como W. E. B. Du Bois ayudaron a entender la raza como parte de la cultura y la identidad, promoviendo la unidad en lugar de la división.

**Próximo paso** – Entender esta historia puede ayudar a la sociedad a seguir rechazando el racismo basado en falsas ciencias. También nos recuerda tener cuidado con investigaciones influenciadas por la política o prejuicios.

**Resumen en una frase** – Los científicos corrigieron mitos dañinos del siglo XIX sobre la raza, demostrando que es una idea social, no un hecho biológico.
